Alsaleem2025.species: Not stated; the model represents a human mandible.
Alsaleem2025.n: Not stated; this is a finite-element model, with no specimen or participant count reported.
Alsaleem2025.loading: Applied perpendicular to the lingual surfaces of the mandibular anterior region and anterior teeth: 1, 7, and 500 g/cm², representing rest, normal function, and abnormal tongue behavior, respectively. No kPa pressures are reported.
Alsaleem2025.measurement: Finite-element outputs were maximum von Mises stress (MPa) and displacement along x, y, and z (mm). Microstrain, slopes, and R² are not stated.
Alsaleem2025.materials: Isotropic properties: cortical bone, Young’s modulus 1.3 MPa and Poisson ratio 0.3; cancellous bone, 1 MPa and 0.3; teeth, 20 MPa and 0.3. Periodontal ligaments were excluded.
Alsaleem2025.solver: Autodesk Inventor was used to create the 3D model and perform stress analysis; a specific solver or version is not stated. Mesh average element size was 0.1 mm; grading factor was 1.5 mm.
Alsaleem2025.boundary_conditions: The mandible was constrained against movement by support on the outer condylar surface, simulating the condyle’s relation to the glenoid fossa.
Alsaleem2025.agreement_metric: Not stated. No experimental validation, cross-solver comparison, strain-gauge data, percentage error, or agreement statistic is reported.
Alsaleem2025.result: Maximum von Mises stresses for 1, 7, and 500 g/cm² were 0.78355, 3.35746, and 177.28 MPa. Reported maximum displacement magnitudes (x, y, z) were 0.0000088295, 0.00000472009, 0.000061563 mm; 0.0000630885, 0.0000340902, 0.000437384 mm; and 0.00432566, 0.0023463, 0.0301568 mm, respectively. No microstrain, slopes, R², or percentage errors are stated.
Alsaleem2025.error_drivers_and_lessons: The authors note that the model does not fully reflect real human structures; bone was modeled as isotropic despite being described as anisotropic and inhomogeneous, and periodontal ligaments were omitted. They caution that results near constraints may be affected by the boundary conditions. No quantified error analysis is stated.
Alsaleem2025.relevance_notes: This study provides a computational example of tongue-related loading on mandibular anterior structures, but it does not test palatal loading, pig tissue, 10–70 kPa pressure, or resting pressures of 0.1–2 kPa. It reports no strain-gauge validation or comparison across FEBio, CalculiX, and JAX, so it supplies no validation errors or agreement metrics for the planned design. Its simplified material assumptions and condylar constraints highlight modeling choices to document and test.

Becker2024.species: Human mandible bone is the subject of the reviewed finite-element studies. The original material-model studies also used other human bone sites and, in one study, steer bone.
Becker2024.n: 77 FE studies were reviewed; 12 distinct heterogeneous material models were identified. The models originated from 10 studies. The review included 31 research groups. No specimen count for the planned pig study is stated.
Becker2024.loading: No single loading condition is reported for the 77 studies. The review covers varied FE applications; specific loads, pressures, and microstrain values are not stated.
Becker2024.measurement: The review examines CT/Hounsfield-unit-derived density–Young’s-modulus relationships. It reports no microstrain measurements, pressure–strain slopes, or numerical R² values. Two representative apparent densities used for comparison were 1.3 g/cm³ (trabecular) and 1.6 g/cm³ (cortical); corresponding commonly used homogeneous moduli were 1.37 GPa and 13.7 GPa.
Becker2024.materials: Bone was modeled with heterogeneous density-dependent Young’s modulus. The 12 models covered trabecular, cortical, or both domains; five were specifically based on human mandible data. Models were derived from femur, tibia, pelvis, multiple bone sites, steer femoral/tibial diaphysis, or mandible.
Becker2024.solver: Not stated. The review reports that 20 studies used Mimics, 1 used Mechanical Finder, 4 used in-house Abaqus subroutines, and 52 did not clearly report the material-assignment toolbox. FEBio, CalculiX, and JAX are not discussed.
Becker2024.boundary_conditions: No specific boundary conditions are reported for the reviewed mandible FE studies. The review notes that original studies differed in test type and setup, including tension versus compression and constrained versus uniaxial loading.
Becker2024.agreement_metric: No FE-to-experiment agreement metric or numerical R² value is provided in the supplied text. The review assessed original-study quality using QUIN and ROBFEAD; reported highest risk scores were 54% for three in-vitro studies and 57% for one FE study.
Becker2024.result: The review found substantial variability among 12 density–modulus models and no consensus on the best mandible model. Reported examples include E = 0.51ρapp^1.37 GPa (Rho et al.); Keyak et al. used E = 33.9ρash^2.2 for ρash ≤ 0.27 g/cm³, E = 5.307ρash + 0.469 for 0.27 < ρash < 0.6, and E = 10.2ρash^2.01 for ρash ≥ 0.6. Mimics default: E = −0.3888 + 5.925ρapp. No percentage prediction errors are reported.
Becker2024.error_drivers_and_lessons: Potential sources of model variation include study type, mechanical-test type and setup, numerical methods and boundary conditions, bone site/domain, sample geometry and size, donor characteristics, and material-assignment method. Twenty-three reports were unavailable. Fifty-two of 77 studies did not clearly identify their assignment toolbox. The Mimics equation’s origin and methodology were unclear; the review advises caution, respecting each model’s density range, bone domain, and directional applicability, and reporting assignment methods.
Becker2024.relevance_notes: This review does not test pig maxilla/palate, palatal pressure, resting tongue pressure, or cross-solver validation, so it supplies no pressure threshold or remodeling evidence for the planned studies. It supports explicitly reporting CT-to-material mapping and testing sensitivity to material models and assignment methods. Its call for standardized protocols and combined simulation–experiment validation is relevant to strain-gauge validation, but the review provides no specific validation error target or loading protocol.

Bright2012.species: Domestic pig (Large White breed), approximately 6 months old; one skull specimen.
Bright2012.n: One specimen (n=1); experimental strain data were averaged over 3 repeated loadings. Sixteen planar rosette gauges were used; G1 and G6 were excluded because their readings were unstable.
Bright2012.loading: A total load of 755 N was applied at the masseter and temporalis attachment sites, approximately equally on the two sides but divided asymmetrically between the muscles. The load pulled the skull onto bilateral tooth and temporomandibular-joint supports.
Bright2012.measurement: Ex vivo planar rosette strain gauges measured principal strain magnitudes, orientations, ratios, and shear strain. Experimental principal strains ranged from +485 με to −606 με. Examples: G5 zygomatic arch, +456/−288 με; G8 squamosal, +68/−606 με; G7 frontal, +485/−196 με. Experimental standard errors were generally 5–10% of the mean.
Bright2012.materials: Bone was modelled as homogeneous, isotropic human cranial cortical bone: E=12.5 GPa, ν=0.35. Sutures were assigned pig nasofrontal suture properties: E=46 MPa, ν=0.35. Teeth had the bone properties. Gauge membranes used E=0.001 GPa, ν=0.35, thickness 0.01 mm.
Bright2012.solver: Abaqus 6.8.2. The mesh contained 1,749,149 quadratic tetrahedral (TET10) elements. Sutures were represented as bands at least 3 elements wide (1.5 mm).
Bright2012.boundary_conditions: Loads were applied through RBE3 rigid-body elements. Teeth were constrained in the dorsoventral (Y) direction; the temporomandibular joints were constrained in all translational directions (XYZ), matching the experimental supports.
Bright2012.agreement_metric: Model–experiment similarity was assessed using Euclidean distance (ED); shorter distances indicate greater similarity. For strain ratio, ED was 3.78 for the no-suture (HOM) model versus 4.86 for the suture (SUT) model. No regression slopes, R² values, or percentage model errors were stated.
Bright2012.result: Adding sutures changed strain magnitudes, ratios, orientations, and contour patterns, particularly in facial/zygomatic regions, but did not improve overall experimental fit and often worsened it. Both models were too stiff, with strains approximately an order of magnitude below experimental values. Strain ratios and orientations were reasonably replicated at most locations; neither model was validated for strain magnitude.
Bright2012.error_drivers_and_lessons: The authors attributed much of the magnitude mismatch to omission of cancellous bone and simplified homogeneous, isotropic bone properties. Cranial bone stiffness varies within and among bones and with loading direction; local bone and suture material-property variation or fusion may also matter. The suture-band approach may absorb strain, but the no-suture model also mismatched data. Validation and controlled isolation of model variables are important.
Bright2012.relevance_notes: This study supports specimen-specific ex vivo validation with known, repeatable loading and matched constraints, and cautions that adding sutures alone may not improve FE accuracy. Its 755 N muscle-attachment loading is not palatal pressure; palatal pressures and resting tongue pressures were not stated. It provides no evidence that 0.1–2 kPa tongue pressure drives remodeling, and does not compare FEBio, CalculiX, or JAX.

Cuff2015.species: Ostrich (Struthio camelus), a farmed subadult aged 6–9 months.
Cuff2015.n: One skull was tested ex vivo. Nanoindentation used samples from a different subadult ostrich; reported indents: bone 59, beak 40, suture 20.
Cuff2015.loading: Bilateral artificial tendons loaded the M. pseudotemporalis superficialis attachment sites. Applied loads after residual-load correction averaged 25.1 N right and 26.3 N left (initially 32 N per side). These were not pressure loads.
Cuff2015.measurement: Strain gauges at 13 skull sites; gauge 6 failed, leaving 12 sites. Two trials; each gauge’s reading averaged 600 recordings over 60 s. Experimental maximum principal strain at G7 was 990 and 970 microstrain; minimum at G5 was −970 and −980 microstrain.
Cuff2015.materials: Isotropic properties. Nanoindentation Young’s modulus: cortical bone mean 5.03 GPa (1.24–9.89); beak mean 0.0271 GPa (0.009–0.067); suture mean 0.018 GPa (0.009–0.046). Trabecular bone was assigned 1.5 GPa in nanoindentation-based models. Poisson’s ratios were assigned, not measured: typically 0.35 for bone/beak and 0.30 for trabecular bone.
Cuff2015.solver: Abaqus 6.8.2; models used Tet10 tetrahedral elements. Mesh selected had 1,749,533 elements. Convergence criteria: successive meshes differed by <10% in gauge-site maximum/minimum strain and <5% in total strain energy.
Cuff2015.boundary_conditions: Two constraints prevented dorsoventral translation at the beak anterior; four constraints on each quadrate prevented movement in all directions. Loads were distributed over 14 nodes at each muscle attachment site. Experimental support was bilateral under the quadrates and at the anterior rhamphotheca.
Cuff2015.agreement_metric: Euclidean distances (smaller indicates greater similarity) and regression tests. Best literature-model distances: L3 for maximum strain 873, minimum strain 556, and orientation 179; L2 for strain ratio 4.04. Slopes and R² values are not stated in the supplied text.
Cuff2015.result: Models generally located peak strains and represented rostral deformation mode, but did not reliably reproduce magnitudes, orientations, or neurocranial deformation mode. Experimental rhamphotheca strains were lower than nearby bone strains; models predicted much higher rhamphotheca principal strains. No single model best matched every metric. Percent validation errors are not stated.
Cuff2015.error_drivers_and_lessons: Potential contributors included isotropic, homogeneous properties despite measured bone modulus variation (1.24–9.89 GPa); uncertain suture geometry/properties; cortical bone or rhamphotheca thickness; specimen dehydration, movement and trial-to-trial loading variation; and artificial-tendon screws. Sutures altered strain patterns and magnitudes. Ex-vivo experiments used one skull; nanoindentation used another.
Cuff2015.relevance_notes: This is a skull-validation precedent, not a pig palate or pressure-loading study: it reports no palatal pressure or tongue-pressure threshold. It supports specimen-specific CT FE validation, explicit modeling of sutures and soft/keratinous tissues, and reporting strain orientations as well as magnitudes. For planned pressure tests, establish actual boundary/load transfer and assess material heterogeneity and hydration; this paper cannot establish whether 0.1–2 kPa tongue pressure remodels maxillary bone.

Daqiq2025.species: Human participants and human cadaveric mandibles; one material-property study used a canine mandible. The review included 66 studies: 60 measuring maximum bite force (MBF), 5 muscle force, and 5 material properties.
Daqiq2025.n: Material-property studies reported 1 canine mandible, 12 TMJ specimens, 5 cadavers, 10 cadavers, and 1 cadaver, respectively. No single pooled sample size was reported for the review’s force measurements.
Daqiq2025.loading: No palatal pressure or kPa loading was reported. Healthy dentulous MBF means: molar 443.6 N (95% CI 384.2–502.9; 35 studies), premolar 428.4 N (371.8–485.0; 5), incisal 209.2 N (132.5–285.9; 18).
Daqiq2025.measurement: Physical bite-force measurements; muscle-force measurements, often using electromyography (EMG); and mechanical testing of cadaveric mandibular bone. Meta-analysis was possible only for MBF. Microstrain, slopes, R², and percentage errors were not stated.
Daqiq2025.materials: Mandible elastic modulus: 4.9–14.5 GPa in studies testing mandible as a whole; cortical bone 10–29.9 GPa; trabecular bone 14.4–33.7 GPa. One TMJ study reported 11.2 MPa in males and 14.3 MPa in females. Other reported values included Poisson ratio 0.1 (range 0.08–0.13) and shear moduli 4.3–8.2 GPa.
Daqiq2025.solver: Not stated. This review included physical tests and excluded in-silico/computational studies.
Daqiq2025.boundary_conditions: Not stated. The review found no physical-test values for mandibular fixation or boundary-condition interactions, including friction and tolerance.
Daqiq2025.agreement_metric: No FE-to-experiment validation agreement metric was reported. Screening agreement was Cohen’s κ = 0.86 (99.51% agreement) for title/abstract screening and κ = 0.61 (80.96% agreement) for full-text screening.
Daqiq2025.result: Healthy dentulous molar MBF was 509.9 N in males and 413.6 N in females; incisal MBF was 295.9 N and 259.1 N, respectively. Molar MBF was 287.3 N below age 20, 470.7 N at 20–60, and 345.0 N above 60. Mandibular bone moduli are reported above; palatal pressure, microstrain, slopes, R², and percent error were not stated.
Daqiq2025.error_drivers_and_lessons: MBF heterogeneity was attributed to differences in sample size, age and sex distributions, and measurement methods. Calibration was reported in only 8 studies; repetition count, biting duration, and rest time also varied. Muscle-force studies used incomparable methods/conditions. Material tests differed in setup and bone region; all included studies had at least two high-risk-of-bias domains.
Daqiq2025.relevance_notes: This human mandibular review supplies no direct ex-vivo pig maxilla/palate data, palatal pressure values, tongue-pressure values, strain-gauge validation results, or solver comparisons. It highlights the need to report specimen and material characteristics, loading/measurement protocols, and validation uncertainty consistently. Its reported bone moduli are mandibular, not validated substitutes for maxillary or palatal properties.

Erdemir2022.species: not stated; the paper evaluates nine computational knee studies and does not identify species in the supplied text.
Erdemir2022.n: 9 studies; 5 reviewer teams; 18 independent reviews. The 14 authors reported more than 160 combined years of experience in finite-element analysis or rigid-body motion simulations.
Erdemir2022.loading: No loading magnitudes or pressures are stated. Boundary-condition information was judged reported in 0.63 [95% CI: 0.56–0.70] of assessments and reproducible in 0.45 [0.39–0.53].
Erdemir2022.measurement: Reviewers assessed reporting and perceived reproducibility using binary yes/no judgments. No microstrain, strain-gauge, slope, or R² measurements are reported.
Erdemir2022.materials: No specific tissue material properties or moduli are reported. The paper notes intersubject variability in tissue material response as a reproducibility challenge.
Erdemir2022.solver: No solver names or solver-specific results are given. The reviewed studies used software ranging from commercially available to lab-specific; software variation could impede reproduction.
Erdemir2022.boundary_conditions: Boundary-condition reporting proportion: 0.63 [95% CI: 0.56–0.70]; perceived reproducibility: 0.45 [0.39–0.53]. Reporting was lower than for subcomponents (0.74 [0.71–0.76]) and interactions (0.79 [0.72–0.86]).
Erdemir2022.agreement_metric: No FE-to-experiment agreement metric, strain comparison, slope, R², or percentage error is reported. The paper used logistic regression to estimate yes-response proportions and 95% confidence intervals.
Erdemir2022.result: Across six major categories, reporting was 0.52 [0.48–0.56] and perceived reproducibility was 0.35 [0.31–0.39]. Category reporting ranged from 0.31 for verification to 0.77 for model structure; reproducibility ranged from 0.22 for verification to 0.44 for model structure. Reproducibility was lower than reporting overall (p < 0.05).
Erdemir2022.error_drivers_and_lessons: The authors identify incomplete reporting, intersubject variability in anatomy, tissue response and loading, complex model development, diverse modeling approaches, limited experimental data, and software variation as challenges. Reviewers judged reproducibility subjectively; the study did not directly reproduce models or assess validation quality.
Erdemir2022.relevance_notes: This review provides no direct evidence about ex vivo pig maxillae, palatal pressures, resting tongue pressure, or bone remodeling. It supports explicitly reporting geometry, material properties, loads, boundary conditions, solver/version, and validation procedures. For the planned strain-gauge comparisons across FEBio, CalculiX, and JAX, report reproducibility assets and quantitative agreement/error metrics; do not treat reported validation alone as proof of reproducibility.

Garavelli2022.species: Human cadaveric lumbar spine from a 73-year-old female (lung cancer with spinal metastasis); not pig.
Garavelli2022.n: One L1–L4 spine segment (n=1); L2 was metastatic and L3 osteoporotic. Displacement validation used 2,452 DIC points: 1,143 on L2 and 1,309 on L3.
Garavelli2022.loading: Compression-flexion; force applied 4 mm anterior to the L2–L3 disc center, reaching 60 N in 1.0 s. Target anterior L3 compressive strain was −2,500 to −3,500 microstrain. Neither palatal pressure nor tongue pressure was tested.
Garavelli2022.measurement: Three-dimensional DIC measured vertebral surface displacement and strain at 25 Hz. Spatial resolution was about 2 mm; displacement systematic and random errors were about 10 μm and 25 μm, respectively. Strain systematic error was 30 microstrain and random error 100 microstrain.
Garavelli2022.materials: Bone: heterogeneous, locally isotropic, linear-elastic brittle; Poisson’s ratio 0.3. CT-derived density was converted to elastic modulus using E=4730·ρapp^1.56 MPa, with ρash=0.079+0.877·ρQCT and ρapp=ρash/0.6. Intervertebral discs: homogeneous isotropic, Poisson’s ratio 0.1; calibrated modulus 1.92 MPa.
Garavelli2022.solver: ANSYS Mechanical APDL V19.3 preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver; parallel distributed memory over 6 cores, 64 GB RAM, Intel Xeon E-2276G 3.80 GHz. Model had 1,198,125 degrees of freedom and took about 2 minutes to solve.
Garavelli2022.boundary_conditions: Inferior surface of L4 fixed; measured superior-pot translations and rotations prescribed remotely at the superior L1 surface through a pilot node using rigid surface-based MPC constraints. The superior pot was experimentally free to rotate and translate via a ball joint and orthogonal low-friction bearings; the inferior pot was fixed.
Garavelli2022.agreement_metric: Local DIC–FE displacement comparison after registration and spatial averaging. R² ranged 0.94–0.98; RMSE 0.028–0.110 mm; normalized RMSE 1.8–7.5%. Slopes: L2 RL/AP/SI 0.823/0.976/1.073; L3 0.650/0.979/1.071. Intercepts: L2 0.054/−0.030/0.054 mm; L3 0.071/−0.023/−0.038 mm.
Garavelli2022.result: The model reproduced vertebral surface displacements under the tested 60 N compression-flexion load. R² exceeded 0.9 and RMSE% was below 8%. Average percentage error was 3.4–8.7% for L2 and 6.4–14.0% for L3 across RL/AP/SI; maximum component errors were 0.077–0.225 mm for L2 and 0.079–0.203 mm for L3. Disc modulus was calibrated to match global experimental stiffness (axial-load difference <0.1%).
Garavelli2022.error_drivers_and_lessons: One specimen limits generalization. Simplified disc properties, omitted posterior ligaments and facet joints, registration error (RMSE 0.53 mm; maximum 2.96 mm), and possible coordinate errors from specimen repositioning may affect predictions. Bone constitutive laws assumed lesions behave as low-density bone; blastic lesions may require different models. Authors recommend more complex disc/joint modelling and future strain-based validation.
Garavelli2022.relevance_notes: Demonstrates a subject-specific CT-based FE validation workflow using measured experimental kinematics, explicit boundary-condition replication, registration-error handling, and local full-field comparison. It supports validating more than global stiffness alone, but uses human spine and DIC—not pig maxilla/palate, strain gauges, or the planned FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparison. No palatal pressure, tongue pressure, or remodeling was studied; the proposed 10–70 kPa and 0.1–2 kPa ranges are not stated here.

Hillam2015.species: Human; one healthy 29-year-old male subject (70 kg).
Hillam2015.n: 1 subject; one functioning right parietal gauge and one tibial gauge. A contralateral parietal gauge did not provide usable central-element data.
Hillam2015.loading: In vivo activities: biting (up to 449 N molar and 430 N incisor bite), chewing a banana, grimacing, walking at ~0.7 m/s, squats with a 25 kg bar, jumps from 0.45 m and 1.3 m, and heading a 4.5 kg ball. Ground-reaction force reached 3,967 N for the 0.45 m jump and 13,242 N for the 1.3 m jump. Palatal pressure was not applied or reported.
Hillam2015.measurement: Three-element rosette strain gauges bonded to bone; strain recorded at 50 Hz for sedentary activities and 500 Hz for vigorous activities. Principal strains calculated from gauge elements. Strain rates used maximum rise over 40 ms. Simultaneous bite-force and force-plate measurements were made when relevant.
Hillam2015.materials: Human parietal bones and right tibia; EA-06-060RZ-120 rosette gauges bonded with cyanoacrylate adhesive. No maxilla or palate specimen, material modulus, or ex vivo material testing reported.
Hillam2015.boundary_conditions: In vivo experimental measurements, not a finite-element model. Strain circuits were zeroed with the subject relaxed: seated with head forward for cranial measurements and seated with foot off the ground for tibial measurements; gauges were re-zeroed between activity sets. No FE boundary conditions reported.
Hillam2015.agreement_metric: not stated; no FE validation, solver comparison, slopes, R² values, or percentage errors reported.
Hillam2015.result: Peak parietal principal strains were 0.0192% tensile and 0.0142% compressive while heading the 4.5 kg ball (192 and 142 με); peak parietal strain rate was 3.225%/s. During grimacing, peaks were 0.0103% and 0.0093% (103 and 93 με). Peak tibial strain in the 1.3 m jump was 0.2066% and 0.0836% (2,066 and 836 με), with a peak rate of 45.525%/s. The authors report physiological peak tibial strain rates above five times parietal rates. No pressure, modulus, slope, or R² values reported.
Hillam2015.error_drivers_and_lessons: Major limitation: a single subject and a single three-element gauge on each bone; the left parietal gauge failed, and the right detached after ball impact. Authors caution that small parietal signals had low signal-to-noise ratio and 40 ms strain-rate estimates could be noise-sensitive; smoothing and lower-resolution checks still showed larger rate differences. No statistical analysis was performed. No percentage error or instrument-validation statistic reported.
Hillam2015.relevance_notes: This is human in vivo parietal-skull evidence, not pig maxilla/palate data: it supplies no palatal pressure–strain relation and does not test resting tongue pressures of 0.1–2 kPa or remodeling. It reports no FE model, material modulus, solver comparison, or validation error. For planned validation, its single-subject, single-gauge limitations underscore the value of multiple measurement sites/repeats and explicit signal-to-noise assessment; its cranial strain magnitudes should not be treated as palatal calibration data.

Jung2010.species: Human subjects; 20 Caucasian adults with normal occlusion (9 males, 11 females; mean age 28.05 years, SD 8.34).
Jung2010.n: 20 participants. Intra-individual repeatability was assessed in 2 subjects with 8 repetitions per run.
Jung2010.loading: Physiological oral-function/posture conditions; no externally applied palatal load. Reported average pressures (IOS, SPS): open-mouth (OC), 0.0 and −0.08 mbar; gently closed lips (SC), −0.16 and −1.0 mbar; closed compartments after negative-pressure generation (CCN), −48.79 and −81.86 mbar; swallowing (SW), −29.25 and −62.51 mbar. Negative pressures of approximately −50 to −150 mbar were observed during CCN and swallowing.
Jung2010.measurement: Simultaneous intra-oral relative-pressure monitoring at the vestibular inter-occlusal space (IOS) and sub-palatal space (SPS), using a piezoresistive sensor (range +100 to −400 mbar; resolution 0.1 mbar). Four phases were recorded: OC 0–30 s, SC 30–90 s, CCN 90–150 s, SW 150–165 s; analysis excluded transition intervals. No microstrain, slopes, or R² reported.
Jung2010.materials: Twenty human participants; polyethylene semi-flexible intravenous catheter and air-permeable dental suction end cap attached to flexible PVC tubing (4 mm internal diameter); GMSD 350 MR piezoresistive relative-pressure sensor. No bone, CT, strain gauges, or material moduli were studied.
Jung2010.solver: not stated; no finite-element solver or computational model was used.
Jung2010.boundary_conditions: Participants seated upright. OC: lips slightly open, quiet breathing; SC: lips gently closed, quiet breathing; CCN: collect and swallow saliva, then quiet breathing after tongue-repositioning/negative-pressure generation; SW: saliva swallowing. Pressure sites were IOS vestibule and SPS beneath the palatal vault. No structural or mechanical support constraints were specified.
Jung2010.agreement_metric: No FE-to-experiment agreement metric. Pressure-curve characteristics were analyzed using non-parametric two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests (α = 0.05). ANOVA phase effects were significant for all curve characteristics (all p < 0.01); measurement-site effects were significant for all characteristics (p = 0.04 to <0.01).
Jung2010.result: The two null hypotheses (no differences by phase and no differences by compartment) were rejected. In CCN, SPS and IOS differed significantly for all curve characteristics (Wilcoxon p < 0.01); during swallowing, average peak height (p = 0.03) and average pressure (p = 0.02) differed. The SPS generally showed larger negative pressures than IOS. No positive pressure peaks or plateaus were observed in the tested conditions. Microstrain, slopes, R², percentage errors, and moduli: not stated.
Jung2010.error_drivers_and_lessons: Repeatability testing in 2 subjects (8 repetitions each) found peak/plateau frequency variation no greater than 2; the largest reported intra-individual IQR was 84.8 mbar for average peak height during CCN. Authors noted that measurement-system pressure loss might provoke repeated SPS-wall activity and could not be excluded. Pressure-curve measures varied substantially, particularly in CCN; no quantified percentage error or calibration agreement was reported.
Jung2010.relevance_notes: This is human physiological pressure evidence, not an ex vivo loading or FE-validation study. It reports negative SPS pressure during swallowing/CCN (average −62.51/−81.86 mbar) and IOS pressure (−29.25/−48.79 mbar), but does not test externally applied 10–70 kPa palatal loading or resting tongue pressure of 0.1–2 kPa. Its two-site measurements support measuring distinct palatal and inter-occlusal compartments; its repeatability observations and acknowledged possible pressure loss caution that sensor placement, sealing, and repeatability should be addressed in validation design.

Liang2024.n: In vivo CT dataset: n=217 children (94 female, 123 male), ages 0–48 months. FE baseline geometry: one 111-day-old female; approximately 5.3 million tetrahedral elements.
Liang2024.loading: No external pressure loading was applied. Growth was simulated by thermal-analogy expansion of intracranial, orbital, nasal-cavity, and upper-intraoral volumes, plus selected skull-base and midfacial bones, over 15 load steps from 3 to 48 months. Palatal pressure and resting tongue pressure were not stated.
Liang2024.measurement: Compared predicted and in-vivo cranial volumes, linear dimensions, circumference, cranial module, cephalic index, mid-facial index, cross-sections, and 3D surface distances. Reported von Mises strain in microstrain (με); no strain-gauge measurements. Numerical regression slopes and R² values are not stated in the text provided.
Liang2024.materials: Isotropic linear-elastic properties at 3 months: bone E=421 MPa, cartilage E=100 MPa, sutures/synchondroses/fontanelles E=30 MPa, intracranial volume E=50 MPa, orbital volumes E=10 MPa, nasal-cavity and upper-intraoral volumes E=421 MPa. Poisson’s ratios: bone/cartilage 0.22, sutures 0.3, volumes/covers 0.1. Bone stiffness increased 125 MPa/month; newly formed tissue, cartilage, and covers increased 100 MPa/month.
Liang2024.solver: Finite-element analysis in ANSYS Mechanical APDL 2022 R2. The model comprised approximately 5.3 million tetrahedral elements. Code was written in ANSYS APDL; solver comparisons with FEBio, CalculiX, or JAX were not stated.
Liang2024.boundary_conditions: One-directional displacement constraints on facial covers; anteroposterior constraints around the basilar occipital bone and dorsoventral constraints around the foramen magnum. Frictional contacts between cranial volumes and inner skeleton used coefficient 0.1, penalty stiffness 100 N/mm for intracranial/orbital contacts and 600 N/mm for nasal/intraoral contacts, and 0.5 mm penetration tolerance. Bone-suture interfaces were bonded.
Liang2024.agreement_metric: Expanded volumes differed by less than 5% from target volumes through 48 months. Approximately 80% of outer-surface distance differences were between −5 mm and +5 mm. Regression significance and R² were shown in figures, but their numerical values and slopes are not stated in the supplied text.
Liang2024.result: Predicted maximum calvarial suture von Mises strain reached 160,000 με at 6 months, almost 8 times the maximum in adjacent calvarial bone. At 24 months, nasal-cavity strain was about 70,000–80,000 με and adjacent maxillary median strain 10,000–35,000 με. At 36 months, nasal-cavity strain exceeded 80,000 με and midface/palate strain was 35,000–65,000 με. The model predicted that skull-base expansion contributes to anteroposterior facial growth and maxillary expansion to dorsoventral facial growth.
Liang2024.error_drivers_and_lessons: The model did not adequately simulate zygomatic-arch growth; posterior cranial-vault underprediction tended to increase with age. Orbital and forehead shape differences exceeded 5 mm from 24 months onward. Authors identify omission of mandible, masticatory and neck muscles, tooth eruption, and molecular/cellular regulation as limitations; these effects were represented partly through regional expansion. Strain predictions omit muscle-action strains. No pressure-response slope or measured validation error for strain was stated.
Liang2024.relevance_notes: This is a human growth model, not an ex-vivo pig maxilla/palate pressure study: it provides no evidence for response to 10–70 kPa palatal loading or 0.1–2 kPa resting tongue pressure, and cannot establish whether tongue pressure drives remodeling. For planned FE validation, it illustrates comparison against independent in-vivo targets, explicit contact/constraint reporting, and reporting of geometric errors; however, it validates morphology rather than strain gauges or cross-solver agreement. Its omission of tongue/muscle forces cautions against treating cavity expansion as measured tongue loading.

Lima2025.species: Human patients/participants; species was not explicitly specified. No animal experiments reported.
Lima2025.n: 24 included studies: 18 primary studies and 6 reviews. The primary studies included 1,050 patients overall, of whom 625 received OMT; for post-orthognathic surgery, 7 studies included 238 participants, with 113 receiving OMT. No single experimental sample for mechanical testing.
Lima2025.loading: No quantified mechanical loading or applied pressure reported. Interventions were orofacial myofunctional exercises, sometimes combined with orthodontic appliances; post-surgery protocols included chewing, swallowing, tongue-position, and other exercises. Pressure values, including palatal or tongue pressures, not stated.
Lima2025.measurement: Clinical function and outcomes, including tongue position, swallowing, lip function, open-bite/overjet measures, cephalometrics, electromyography, masticatory efficiency, occlusal contacts/force, jaw movement, and quality of life. Microstrain, strain-gauge measurements, and FE outputs not stated.
Lima2025.materials: No mechanical test materials or tissue material properties reported. Elastic moduli and other constitutive properties not stated.
Lima2025.result: Scoping review of 24 studies (18 primary, 6 reviews); only 4 primary studies (22%) were RCTs. Six comparisons were considered plausible: five had Level 3 evidence and one Level 2; none had Level 1 evidence. OMT after orthognathic surgery had Level 2 evidence of possible benefit. No microstrain, slope, R², percentage error, modulus, or pressure results reported.
Lima2025.error_drivers_and_lessons: The review identifies weak study methods as key limitations: inadequate or undescribed randomization, absent allocation concealment, open-label designs, small samples, and short follow-up. OMT protocols and provider expertise varied or were not reported. These limit confidence in treatment-effect estimates; no quantitative mechanical-validation errors were assessed.
Lima2025.relevance_notes: This clinical scoping review provides no data on ex vivo pig maxilla/palate loading, palatal pressure ranges, CT-based FE validation, FEBio/CalculiX/JAX comparisons, or whether resting tongue pressure drives bone remodeling. It supports distinguishing clinical evidence from biomechanical validation and highlights the need for well-designed, clearly specified protocols, controls, and outcomes; it cannot supply loading values or validation benchmarks for the planned studies.

Liu2026.n: Control: n=8 (half each sex). Tongue-base reduction: n=6; enlargement: n=6. Experimental animals were same-sex sibling pairs, half each sex.
Liu2026.loading: No applied mechanical pressure was reported. Tongue-base volume was reduced by coblation by 1.20 ± 0.48 cm³ (4%–8%); enlargement was induced by high-calorie feeding to obesity (BMI >51).
Liu2026.measurement: Postmortem skull measurements: 99 landmarks and 51 linear distances; tongue and masseter dimensions, weights, and volumes. No microstrain, pressure, slope, or modulus reported.
Liu2026.materials: Yucatan minipig skulls, tongues, and bilateral masseters; tongue-base tissue was ablated in the reduction group. No ex vivo maxilla/palate specimens or strain gauges reported.
Liu2026.agreement_metric: No FE-to-experiment agreement metric reported. Measurement reliability: inter-investigator ICC=0.989; intra-investigator ICC=0.996; Dahlberg measurement error=0.15 mm.
Liu2026.result: Reduction group had smaller midfacial width (p=0.035), maxillary inter-canine width (p<0.001), and mandibular ramus height (p=0.028) than controls. Enlargement group had smaller mandibular inter-canine, first-premolar, and posterior inter-molar widths than controls (p<0.05). Reduction-group tongue-base width correlated with inter-canine width (r=−0.91, p=0.012); no microstrain, slopes, R², or moduli reported.
Liu2026.error_drivers_and_lessons: Controls were 5 weeks younger; their measurements were age-normalized using an 18.6% increase. Controls were euthanized 3 weeks after arrival, experimental animals after 7 weeks. These design and normalization choices matter when comparing group differences. No FE error or validation results were reported.
Liu2026.relevance_notes: This study reports skeletal associations with altered tongue volume, not effects of resting tongue pressure or applied palatal pressure; it cannot establish whether 0.1–2 kPa drives remodeling. It provides no evidence for 10–70 kPa loading, strain-gauge validation, or comparisons among FEBio, CalculiX, and JAX. Its reported landmark-measurement repeatability may inform measurement-quality checks, but it is not FE validation.

MehariAbraha2019.species: One female rhesus macaque (Macaca mulatta); the study used a subject-specific mandible model. In vivo validation data came from this individual. Three strain-gauge sites were used.
MehariAbraha2019.n: One animal; 3 strain-gauge sites (ULAT, LLAT, MED). Table 1 reports 148 in vivo observations per gauge location and 24–56 FE surface elements per model/site. These are not independent animal sample sizes.
MehariAbraha2019.loading: Subject-specific muscle-force vectors simulated unilateral left post-canine chewing on nuts. Forces were estimated from in vivo EMG and muscle PCSA, scaled using muscle-specific tension of 30 N/cm². No palatal pressure or tongue-pressure loading was applied.
MehariAbraha2019.measurement: Maximum and minimum principal bone strains (ε1, ε2; με), principal-strain orientations, and sagittal, frontal, and transverse shear strains. Validation gauges were on the working-side corpus: upper lateral (ULAT), lower lateral (LLAT), and medial (MED).
MehariAbraha2019.materials: PDL modeled as homogeneous, isotropic, linear elastic; baseline E=0.68 MPa, ν=0.49. Sensitivity models used E=0.07, 0.18, 13.8, and 1,750 MPa. No-PDL model assigned the PDL space tooth properties: E=24,500 MPa, ν=0.49. Teeth: E=24,500 MPa, ν=0.49; trabecular tissue: E=10,000 MPa, ν=0.3; bone screws: E=105,000 MPa, ν=0.36. Cortical bone had 80 heterogeneous orthotropic properties.
MehariAbraha2019.solver: Abaqus CAE Simulia v2016, default implicit direct static solver; approximately 10 minutes per model using 4 processors and 8 tokens.
MehariAbraha2019.boundary_conditions: Working-side left premolars and first molar occlusal surfaces fixed against translation in all directions. Working-side condyle fixed against translation in all directions; balancing-side condyle fixed anterior-posteriorly and superior-inferiorly but allowed medio-lateral translation. Rotation allowed at both condyles. Adjacent internal surfaces were tied.
MehariAbraha2019.agreement_metric: Compared FE principal-strain magnitudes and orientations with in vivo gauge data. In 2/3 sites, median principal-strain magnitudes from both models were within 1.5×IQR of in vivo data; at MED, only PDL-model ε2 met that criterion. Both models’ principal-strain orientations were within the in vivo range at all 3 sites. No R², slope, or percentage error was reported.
MehariAbraha2019.result: Including the PDL affected local and global strains, but effects away from alveoli were generally limited to approximately 200–300 με. Across PDL E=0.07–1,750 MPa, global surface strains changed little. Excluding PDL reduced strains in many alveolar-bone regions by >200 με and shear strains locally by >500 με, while tooth-root principal-strain differences exceeded ~250 με and reached >~500 με. PDL/no-PDL models both generally fell within in vivo ranges.
MehariAbraha2019.error_drivers_and_lessons: The study notes sensitivity may depend on bite location, species and mandibular geometry, muscle activation/loading, and condylar boundary conditions. Its CT resolution was 0.2 mm, insufficient to resolve reported PDL thickness variation (~0.05–0.5 mm); PDL was represented as a simplified space. Static linear modeling omits time-dependent behavior. Validation was partial: MED ε1 magnitudes were not within 1.5×IQR for either model.
MehariAbraha2019.relevance_notes: This is a mandibular chewing study, not an ex vivo pig maxilla/palate test; it provides no palatal pressure, tongue-pressure, remodeling, or cross-solver comparison data. It supports validating FE predictions against strain gauges and reporting site-specific agreement rather than assuming global validation. For planned pressure studies, test sensitivity to material properties, geometry/resolution, loading, and boundary conditions; its 200–300 με away-from-alveoli finding cannot be transferred quantitatively to palatal loading.

Profico2024.n: 51 CT scans were analysed for muscle cross-sectional areas; six age-representative skulls (3, 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 months) were used for finite-element models. The source database contained 217 individuals.
Profico2024.loading: Estimated bilateral temporalis, masseter and medial pterygoid peak forces, based on muscle cross-sectional area × 37 N cm−2; temporal-fascia forces estimated by sensitivity tests. Simulated bilateral first-molar bites, bilateral central-incisor bites and unilateral left first-molar bites. No palatal pressure was applied.
Profico2024.measurement: FE-predicted von Mises strain and stress across cranial bones and joints, plus bite and temporomandibular-joint reaction forces. Facial-region maximum strain during bilateral first-molar biting decreased from about 10,000 µε at 3 months to 100 µε at 48 months. No strain-gauge measurements, strain slopes, or R² values are stated.
Profico2024.materials: Linear-elastic isotropic properties: at 3 months, bone modulus 421 MPa and cranial-joint modulus 30 MPa; Poisson’s ratios 0.22 and 0.3, respectively. Moduli increased by 125 MPa month−1 for bone through 48 months and 100 MPa month−1 for joints through 12 months. No pressure-dependent material properties are stated.
Profico2024.solver: ANSYS v2022 R2. Models had approximately 1.1–1.6 million tetrahedral elements. No other solver or cross-solver comparison is stated.
Profico2024.boundary_conditions: Biting points constrained against translation in all three axes, without rotational constraints; paired TMJ nodes similarly constrained in all three axes. Before tooth eruption, bite points were estimated alveolar eruption sites. Muscle forces were applied at origin nodes along estimated vectors. Temporal-fascia forces were applied at the zygomatic arch, without equal-and-opposite forces at the temporal lines.
Profico2024.agreement_metric: Predicted maximum bite forces at 36–48 months were within the lower range of published in-vivo data but approximately 21–32% lower. Alternative TMJ constraint approaches changed bite and TMJ reaction forces by less than 5%. No R², strain-validation error, or formal agreement statistic is stated.
Profico2024.result: Mean per-side forces rose from 3 to 48 months: temporalis 30.9 to 87.0 N, masseter 25.6 to 69.6 N, medial pterygoid 23.1 to 58.9 N. Maximum bilateral first-molar bite force rose from 90.5 N at 3 months to 184.2 N at 48 months without fascia, and from 78.5 to 165.0 N with fascia. Facial strain was higher than calvarial/skull-base strain; stress generally increased with age. Fascia reduced bite-force estimates 10–15%.
Profico2024.error_drivers_and_lessons: The authors identify muscle-force estimation from anatomical rather than physiological cross-sectional area, omitted muscle architecture (including pennation), limited CT resolution, simplified muscle segmentation, linear-isotropic material assumptions, and omitted brain/eye interactions as limitations. Bite forces were lower than published in-vivo values by approximately 21–32%. The fascia setup omitted reaction at temporal lines, reducing predicted bite force; no quantitative strain-validation error is reported.
Profico2024.relevance_notes: This is human cranial FE work, not an ex-vivo pig maxilla/palate study: it supplies no palatal pressure levels, strain-gauge validation, or evidence about whether 0.1–2 kPa resting tongue pressure drives remodeling. For planned validation, its <5% constraint-sensitivity result and 21–32% bite-force discrepancy illustrate the need to report boundary-condition sensitivity and compare predictions with measurements. It does not compare FEBio, CalculiX or JAX.

Rooks2022.species: Human knee models; four previously developed models derived from cadaveric MRI and laxity datasets. Species is not explicitly stated.
Rooks2022.n: 4 tibiofemoral FE models: du02, oks001, oks003, and oks006. The study performed 101 varus and valgus simulations per model for each parameter analysis.
Rooks2022.loading: Each simulation brought the joint into contact, applied 0.5 body weight axial load, then applied varus or valgus moments of 40 Nm (40,000 Nmm). Contact-pressure analysis used a converged time step later than 2.25, corresponding to at least 10,000 Nmm applied moment.
Rooks2022.measurement: Assessed convergence, valgus kinematics, peak tibial-cartilage contact pressure, and peak-pressure location. Kinematic difference was RMSE in degrees; pressure difference was percentage; peak-location difference was distance in mm. No microstrain, strain-gauge measurements, or validation slopes/R² were reported.
Rooks2022.materials: Ligaments were Neo-Hookean; menisci were Fung-orthotropic; bones and cartilages were rigid. Ligament Young’s modulus was varied by ±100 MPa from model-specific calibrated values, in 25 MPa steps. Meniscus horn springs were varied from the original 1 N/mm to 5, 10, and 20 N/mm per spring.
Rooks2022.solver: FEBio 3.0.0. Models were generated using FEBioStudio 1.0.0. The paper did not compare FEBio with CalculiX or JAX.
Rooks2022.boundary_conditions: Rigid cylindrical joints prescribed loads or displacements in six knee-joint degrees of freedom. Ligaments were rigidly tied to bone meshes; articulating cartilage and menisci used sliding-elastic contact. Simulations included axial loading and varus/valgus moments. No ex vivo maxilla/palate boundary conditions were used.
Rooks2022.agreement_metric: No cross-solver or experimental validation agreement metric was reported. Sensitivity comparisons used kinematic RMSE, percentage differences in peak contact pressure and convergence time, and distances between peak-pressure locations. Qualitative influence scores ranged from 0 (none) to 3 (large).
Rooks2022.result: Ligament prestretch, Young’s modulus, and attachment conditions affected outcomes; sensitivity was generally model-dependent. Meniscus horn stiffness had a small influence. Augmented Lagrangian contact increased peak pressure substantially; for oks003, the average increase was 2,454%. Auto-penalty and search-radius changes prevented simulations from reaching the loading phase in all models.
Rooks2022.error_drivers_and_lessons: Convergence depended on model and parameter; changing the Quasi-Newton method prevented convergence in du02 and oks006, while changing the rigid-joint moment penalty caused convergence failures in all but oks003. Contact formulation and penalty choices strongly affected pressure; disabling two-pass contact produced unrealistic penetration. Different convergence times meant analyzed simulations could have different applied loads.
Rooks2022.relevance_notes: This is not a palatal-loading, bone-strain, strain-gauge, or tongue-pressure study; it reports no microstrain, moduli for maxillary bone, pressure-response slopes, R², or percentage validation errors. It supports testing solver/contact and boundary-condition sensitivity and reporting convergence alongside outputs. Its model-specific sensitivities caution against assuming one FEBio result transfers to CalculiX or JAX. Its 0.5-body-weight and 40 Nm knee loads are not comparable to planned 10–70 kPa palatal or 0.1–2 kPa tongue pressures.

Valeri2024.species: Pig (hard-palate specimens obtained from a local butcher shop); number of animals or palate specimens not stated.
Valeri2024.n: 189 tests: 7 screw types × 3 loading directions (pull-out, push-in, shear) × 3 insertion torques (25, 30, 35 N·cm) × 3 repetitions. Number of pig specimens not stated.
Valeri2024.loading: Displacement-controlled tests at 0.1 mm/s; insertion torques 25, 30, and 35 N·cm. No palatal pressure or pressure loading was applied. FE case applied 1 N at the screw head.
Valeri2024.measurement: Universal testing machine measured force and displacement. Capacity was maximum force (Fmax); secant stiffness was Fmax/dmax. Reported force ranges: pull-out 303.65–791.19 N, push-in 346.43–1229.14 N, and shear 13.09–42.08 N. Strain gauges, microstrain, slopes, and R² were not stated.
Valeri2024.materials: Seven self-drilling titanium or Ti-6Al-4V mini-screws: diameters 1.5–2 mm and lengths 7–15.1 mm. Screw Young’s moduli: 105 GPa (titanium) and 108 GPa (Ti-6Al-4V). FE model values: trabecular bone 1.5 GPa, cortical bone 14.7 GPa, tooth 20.7 GPa, periodontal ligament 6.89×10⁻⁵ GPa, and mini-screw 114 GPa.
Valeri2024.solver: ANSYS was used for the 3D finite-element model. The oral-cavity anatomy used solid elements; mini-screws were represented as Winkler beams with subgrade stiffness. FEBio, CalculiX, and JAX were not used.
Valeri2024.boundary_conditions: Screws were inserted perpendicular to the maxillary bone’s perpendicular plate in pig palate held in a custom steel fixture. FE interface properties included screw–bone friction coefficient 0.3, tooth–bone 0.37, and bonded PDL–tooth and PDL–bone interfaces. FE loading was 1 N at the screw head.
Valeri2024.agreement_metric: No experimental–FE validation comparison, agreement statistic, R², or percent error was reported. Coefficients of variation for repeated test results were reported, generally about 0.05–0.15.
Valeri2024.result: Mean derived ultimate shear stress for pull-out was 7.79, 9.04, and 9.52 MPa at 25, 30, and 35 N·cm; push-in values were 12.06, 10.76, and 13.56 MPa; shear values were 1.64, 3.43, and 3.82 MPa. Mean embedment stiffness (N/mm³) was respectively 2.67, 2.71, 3.09 (pull-out); 17.47, 14.23, 19.65 (push-in); and 0.42, 0.42, 0.45 (shear). The 1 N FE load produced an 8 N screw force and about 0.01 mm displacement.
Valeri2024.error_drivers_and_lessons: Repeat-test CoVs indicate measurable variability (approximately 0.05–0.15); the paper does not identify quantified error sources or report FE validation error. Torque, screw geometry, and loading direction affected measured performance; ANOVA found torque especially influential for push-in outcomes, length for pull-out capacity, and diameter for shear stiffness. Biological variability and fixture effects were not quantified.
Valeri2024.relevance_notes: This is directly relevant as ex vivo pig-palate mini-screw testing, but it measures screw pull-out, push-in, and shear—not distributed palatal pressure or bone strain. It provides no evidence about resting tongue pressures of 0.1–2 kPa or remodeling. For the planned 10–70 kPa pressure study, it offers a fixture/testing precedent but no pressure-to-strain calibration. Its FE work was not validated against measurements, underscoring the value of strain-gauge validation and cross-solver comparison.

Walmsley2013.species: Seven crocodilian taxa: Crocodylus intermedius, C. johnstoni, C. moreletii, C. novaeguineae, Mecistops cataphractus, Osteolaemus tetraspis, and Tomistoma schlegelii. This study concerns skull/mandible models, not pig maxilla or palate.
Walmsley2013.n: 7 species; each FE model contained >1 million elements. Number of specimens per species: not stated.
Walmsley2013.loading: Simulated biting, shaking, and twisting. Biting used muscle-beam pretension; shaking applied forces to four teeth at the selected bite position; twisting restrained those teeth and applied torque at the occipital condyle. Loads were not specified in kPa. Resting tongue pressure and palatal pressure were not studied.
Walmsley2013.measurement: Primary outcome: 95th-percentile von Mises strain (the highest elemental strain after excluding the upper 5%); reported in microstrain. Exact absolute strain values are not provided in the supplied text. Strain magnitude was assessed, not tensile/compressive type or anatomical location.
Walmsley2013.materials: Isotropic heterogeneous (HU-based) versus isotropic homogeneous bone properties. Homogeneous properties for every species were taken from M. cataphractus: Young’s modulus 13,471 MPa and density 1.58×10^-9 T/mm³. Heterogeneous values used empirically derived bovine-femur data and a modified HU relationship; element-level modulus values are not stated.
Walmsley2013.solver: Strand7; CT data processed in MIMICS v11, surface meshes generated/optimized and solid meshes produced using Harpoon. FEBio, CalculiX, and JAX were not used.
Walmsley2013.boundary_conditions: Biting: teeth restrained at front, mid, or back positions and adductor muscle beams pretensioned. Shaking: direct force on four engaged teeth. Twisting: engaged teeth restrained and torque applied at the caudal-most occipital-condyle node. Detailed constraint sets and numerical load magnitudes: not stated.
Walmsley2013.agreement_metric: Compared paired-condition absolute percentage differences, interspecies rankings, standardized strain patterns, and standardized pattern difference (SPD). No strain-gauge or other empirical validation agreement metric, regression slope, or validation R² was reported.
Walmsley2013.result: Heterogeneous versus homogeneous properties produced mean percentage differences of 1.71–11.86% across species; rankings were identical or differed by only two species in 46/54 condition pairs. Volume versus surface scaling averaged about 5% difference; length scaling differed more. Bite-position comparisons averaged 26.93–47.82% (front–mid), 44.93–65.90% (front–back), and 28.75–38.62% (mid–back) across species. LLC sensitivity varied by condition; mean differences reached 30.57% for length-scaled biting. No pressure values, slopes, or validation R² were reported.
Walmsley2013.error_drivers_and_lessons: Functional assumptions dominated: bite position and linear load-case choice altered results more than the tested material-property regime or volume-versus-surface scaling. Length scaling changed outcomes more than volume/surface scaling; effects interacted with feeding behavior and skull shape. Bite-position comparisons had large differences and often changed rankings. LLC percentage differences correlated with shape ΔPC2 (R²=0.77; ΔPC1 R²=0.21); length-versus-volume scaling correlations were R²=0.85 for ΔPC2 and 0.39 for ΔPC1. These are shape correlations, not validation statistics.
Walmsley2013.relevance_notes: This crocodilian skull/mandible sensitivity study does not establish FE accuracy for ex vivo pig maxilla/palate, quantify palatal pressure response, or test resting tongue pressure or remodeling. Its lesson for the planned work is to model biologically justified loading locations and boundary conditions, and test sensitivity to load placement and load definition rather than assuming consistent inputs guarantee robust comparative results. Validate the pig model directly against strain gauges and report errors/agreement across solvers; none of the requested pressures (10–70 kPa or 0.1–2 kPa), solver comparisons, or remodeling outcomes is stated here.

Xiao2026.species: Humans: children aged 4–7 years with mild oral habits; no animal or ex vivo specimens.
Xiao2026.n: 64 children total: intervention n=32 and control n=32. Five were lost to follow-up (3 intervention, 2 control); reported analyses used intention-to-treat with last observation carried forward.
Xiao2026.loading: No mechanical pressure or force was applied or quantified. The intervention was 12 months of myofunctional exercises plus habit-cessation counseling; controls received counseling only. Palatal pressures of 10–70 kPa and resting tongue pressures of 0.1–2 kPa are not stated or tested.
Xiao2026.measurement: Dental impressions at baseline, 6, and 12 months were scanned for maxillary intercanine width, intermolar width, arch perimeter, and palatal depth. At 12 months, intervention vs control changes were: ICW +3.42±1.18 vs +1.87±0.95 mm; IMW +2.76±1.04 vs +1.45±0.88 mm; perimeter +4.28±1.56 vs +2.34±1.21 mm; depth −0.48±0.62 vs +0.12±0.54 mm.
Xiao2026.materials: Alginate impressions (Tropicalgin, Zhermack), Type IV dental stone, 3Shape D700 laboratory scanner, and 3Shape OrthoAnalyzer software. No strain gauges or CT-derived models are described.
Xiao2026.solver: Not stated; no finite-element analysis or FEBio, CalculiX, or JAX solver was used.
Xiao2026.boundary_conditions: Not stated; no computational or mechanical boundary conditions are described.
Xiao2026.agreement_metric: No FE-to-experiment agreement metric, slope, R², or percentage error is reported. Examiner repeat-measurement reliability was reported as ICC >0.90.
Xiao2026.result: Between-group differences in 12-month changes: ICW 1.55 mm (95% CI 1.02–2.08; p<0.001; Cohen’s d=1.45); IMW 1.31 mm (0.83–1.79; p<0.001; d=1.36); arch perimeter 1.94 mm (1.25–2.63; p<0.001; d=1.39); palatal depth −0.60 mm (−0.89 to −0.31; p<0.001; d=1.02). Habit cessation: 87.5% vs 65.6% (p=0.038).
Xiao2026.error_drivers_and_lessons: The authors note possible selection bias from quasi-random allocation by recruitment week, lack of allocation concealment, incomplete blinding, parent-reported habit/adherence outcomes, single-center design, small pilot sample, and possible confounding by growth and tooth eruption. No numerical measurement-error percentage, model error, or mechanical uncertainty is reported.
Xiao2026.relevance_notes: This clinical study reports arch-dimension changes associated with myofunctional training, but provides no measured tongue pressure, ex vivo palatal loading, strain, bone remodeling endpoint, or FE validation data. It cannot establish whether 0.1–2 kPa resting tongue pressure drives remodeling or inform behavior under 10–70 kPa loading. Its use of repeated outcomes and a control group is relevant conceptually; the reported ICC >0.90 concerns examiner measurement repeatability, not FE validation.
